title: Comprehensive Opioid Management and Breathing During Sleep
official: Respiratory Effects of Dose Optimization Under Comprehensive Opioid Management (REDUCE)
summary:
The REDUCE study will evaluate whether referral to a comprehensive opioid management program improves breathing stability during sleep in adults with chronic opioid use and sleep-disordered breathing.

This is a Phase II, single-center, randomized, controlled study. Participants will be randomly assigned to either usual care or referral to the UC San Diego Opioid Management Program. Participants referred to the program will receive individualized opioid and pain management from their treating clinician or designated opioid management provider. Treatment may include changes to opioid medications and other pain-management strategies when clinically appropriate. The research team will not prescribe opioids or direct opioid dose adjustments, and no opioid dose reductions are required by the study.

Participants will be followed for approximately 26 weeks. Study assessments will include overnight sleep studies, questionnaires, blood collection, psychomotor vigilance testing, and regular safety monitoring.

The primary objective is to determine whether comprehensive opioid management improves ventilatory stability compared with usual care.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Age 18 to 75 years.

Chronic opioid use for ≥3 months with a daily dose ≥20 mg oral morphine-equivalent (MEqD).

Diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), defined as AASM-recommended apnea-hypopnea index (AHI3A) ≥5 events per hour on a qualifying sleep study. AHI3A includes hypopnea definition ≥30% airflow reduction lasting ≥10 seconds, accompanied by ≥3% SpO₂ desaturation or arousal.

Ability and willingness to comply with all study procedures, including overnight polysomnography and follow-up.

Ability to provide written informed consent.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Known severe pulmonary disease (e.g., advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) that, in the opinion of the investigator, may increase the risk of oxygen-induced hypercapnia.

Unstable or clinically significant cardiopulmonary disease, including but not limited to decompensated heart failure, unstable angina, or clinically significant arrhythmia.

Recent hospitalization (within the past 30 days) or anticipated need for hospitalization during the study period.

Recreational or non-prescribed opioid use.

Alcohol use exceeding 2 standard drinks per day or evidence of substance use disorder that may interfere with study participation.

Presence of other sleep disorders or neurologic conditions that significantly affect breathing during sleep (e.g., neuromuscular disease), in the opinion of the investigator.

Uncontrolled insomnia.

Pregnancy or breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant during the study period.

Inability to tolerate study procedures, including overnight polysomnography.

Inability to provide informed consent or comply with study procedures.

Any medical, psychiatric, or social condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would interfere with safe participation or interpretation of study results.

Inability to safely participate in Comprehensive Opioid Management.

Unstable or uncontrolled pain conditions.

Recent significant changes in opioid regimen.
